rows.speaker: Mujāhid and Ibn ‘Abbās (rta)
rows.claim: Islahi reports their view that a person may slip into sin but soon emerges from it.
rows.anchor: ascribed to Mujāhid and Ibn ‘Abbās (rta)26 is that a person stumbles into a sin but then soon comes out of this state.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A sinless life is not required; faith should keep sin from taking over, so a person reforms as soon as he recognizes a lapse, and God forgives such people.
rows.anchor: it is not required of a person to lead a sinless life. A person may at times while succumbing to emotions and desires commit a sin; however,

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He cites 4:17–18 to distinguish forgiveness for prompt repentance from the unaccepted repentance of lifelong sinners and those who die disbelieving.
rows.anchor: It is they who are forgiven by God. God is all-knowing and wise.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He defines ithm as sins involving usurpation of rights, oppression, and injustice.
rows.anchor: sins which relate to usurpation of rights, oppression and injustice

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He defines fawāḥish as open indecencies and sexual transgressions.
rows.anchor: open indecencies and sexual transgressions.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Avoiding major sins does not exempt minor sins; strong faith prevents persistence in them, like a trusted person would not tolerate dishonesty over a small sum.
rows.anchor: so strong is the sense of faith of people who safeguard themselves from major sins that they never remain adamant on minor ones.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning addresses people mired in sin who expect Paradise through alleged deities, noble ancestors, or racial superiority; faith and righteous deeds alone avail them before God.
rows.anchor: what is going to be of avail to them before God is faith and righteous deeds and not this false support.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says Quraysh and the People of the Book held false notions, while Quraysh also took pride in lineage and custodianship of the House of God.
rows.anchor: both the Quraysh and the People of the Book were inflicted with some sort of false notion or the other.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh pride in Abrahamic descent and Kaaba custodianship is answered with 9:19: pilgrim services cannot replace faith and righteous deeds or conceal crimes.
rows.anchor: yet this cannot take the place of embracing faith and doing righteous deeds nor one which can conceal their crimes.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The People of the Book imagined their descent from Abraham and Isaac exempted them from Hell, or limited any punishment to a few days.
rows.anchor: since they were the chosen people and were the descendents of Abraham (sws) and Isaac (sws), the fire of Hell would not touch them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jesus warned them against boasting of Abrahamic descent, saying God could raise Abraham’s progeny from stones (Matthew 3:9).
rows.anchor: not show conceit on being the progeny of Abraham (sws) and that if his Lord wanted, he could create Abraham’s progeny from stones.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims followed this Jewish conceit, treating themselves as automatically forgiven; some families and graveyards were regarded as guaranteeing Paradise regardless of belief or deeds.
rows.anchor: Muslims too regarded themselves to be forgiven people and had thereby absolved themselves of all the responsibilities related to faith and deeds.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse warns such people not to declare themselves holy: God knows their earthly and embryonic origins, and rank comes through faith and virtue, not bodily form.
rows.anchor: all people who have this mentality are addressed and warned that they should not regard themselves to be holy and indulge in self-praise.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God alone knows and measures each person’s worth, so no one may proclaim high status before His judgment; Islahi points ahead to 70:38–39.
rows.anchor: It is He who will measure things by His scale and grant each person the status he deserves.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi uses the verse’s degrading description of human origins to challenge waḥdat al-wujūd: if humans are part of God, why describe them so disparagingly?
rows.anchor: If man is really a part of God, then did the Almighty refer to one His parts, God forbid, in such a degrading way in this verse?

rows.speaker: Sufis
rows.claim: Islahi rejects the Sufi self-praise “I am pure and flawless; what majesty I have,” as arrogant and incompatible with the verse’s rebuke of self-exaltation.
rows.anchor: these Sufis chant: ﺳﺒﺤﺎI am pure and flawless! What majesty I have! Exalted is my majesty).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says Sufis imported this creed from the Bāṭiniyya, extremist Shiites, and Brahmans rather than Qur’an and Hadith, and many repeat it without understanding.
rows.anchor: since the Sufis instead of receiving guidance from the Qur’ ān and Ḥadīth have received it from the bātaniyyah, extremist Shiites and the Brahmans

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verses portray miserly people who give little, yet presume a high rank in the Hereafter; Islahi asks whether they can see the unseen to know their promised status.
rows.anchor: Do they have a telescope which is capable of seeing the matters of the unseen world

rows.speaker: our exegetes
rows.claim: Exegetes generally identify the person in the passage as Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah, a Quraysh chief, and recount his abandoned plan to embrace Islam.
rows.anchor: Our exegetes generally regard ﻟﺬيۡ to be a reference to Wal īd ibn al-Mughīrah

rows.speaker: our exegetes
rows.claim: Exegetes report that a companion promised to shield Walīd from the Hereafter if he paid money; Walīd abandoned conversion, promised payment, then paid only part.
rows.anchor: Though this incident has been cited by all our exegetes,

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says the report has no sound chain and, even if true, its connection to these verses is unclear; the Qur’an is not rebuking Walīd for breaking a promise.
rows.anchor: in the first place it does not have a sound chain of narration, and if it is supposed that this incident is true

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He criticizes exegetes for treating the generic relative al-ladhī or al as a proper noun, then inventing a person and an ill-fitting incident to explain it.
rows.anchor: they start looking for a person whom these words qualify.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relative forms al-ladhī and al can also introduce a parable that portrays a group’s collective character through a specific figure.
rows.anchor: at certain instances, they are used to portray a parable too. At such instances, the purpose is to present the collective character of a group

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The woman in 16:92 who unravels her spun thread is a symbolic example, not a particular old woman whose identity and biography need investigation.
rows.anchor: it does not refer to a specific old lady so that one may start investigating her name, family and whereabouts

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hypothetical miserly idolater represents Arabs who refuse to spend yet expect Paradise through alleged deities and racial superiority; Walīd, Abū Jahl, and other wealthy Quraysh see themselves in it.
rows.anchor: a hypothetical character is portrayed to the Idolaters of Arabia.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discourse uses disparaging, sarcastic irony toward people who give grudgingly yet act as if they can already see Paradise’s luxuries.
rows.anchor: The style of the discourse in these verses is disparaging and sarcastic:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word akdā comes from an idiom for a digger striking a large rock too difficult to break.
rows.anchor: which means that such a big rock was encountered by a digger that breaking it was difficult for him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idiom depicts misers who give little under pressure, clench their fists, and attack anyone urging them to spend; 90:6 portrays their boast of having squandered heaps of money.
rows.anchor: if they spend out of compulsion, they spend very little and at that time are overcome by stinginess so much that they clench their fists

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh and People of the Book dream of Paradise through alleged intercession, but the teachings of Moses and Abraham say no soul bears another’s burden.
rows.anchor: in the Hereafter no soul shall bear the burden of another?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The primary addressees are Quraysh and, secondarily, the People of the Book: the latter claimed Moses and Abraham, while Quraysh treated Abraham as ancestor and religious leader.
rows.anchor: the addressees here are primarily the Quraysh and secondarily the People of the Book.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham is called one who fulfilled: he obeyed every divine directive, kept his promise, and passed every trial; 2:124 likewise says he fulfilled his test.
rows.anchor: fulfilled his promise and who passed every test and trial in an outstanding way.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham’s high standing came from complete obedience and faithfulness, whereas his descendants seek his favor without obeying God.
rows.anchor: the high status achieved by Abraham (sws) in this world and in the next was the result of showing complete obedience and faithfulness to God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham had no formal scripture; teachings were transmitted orally to both branches, preserved better among Israelites through prophets, blurred among illiterate Ishmaelites, and later included and partly altered in the Torah.
rows.anchor: he did not have a scripture in the formal sense of the term. All his teachings were transmitted orally as traditions
